subject: Science
title: Farmer Ravi's Smart Harvest
hook: How does a farmer grow rice to feed India? Learn the secrets of crop production.

characters.name: Maya
characters.role: Ravi's curious daughter who studies soil science

slides.title: Ravi's Fields
slides.storyContext: Farmer Ravi owns 2 acres in Punjab. He grows rice and wheat but doesn't always get good yields. His daughter Maya, in Class 8, asks: 'Papa, why don't we grow more food? The whole village depends on our crops.' Ravi decides it's time to learn the right way. Their neighbour Gopal, an agricultural scientist, offers to help them understand modern farming.

slides.title: What Crops Need: Soil Preparation
slides.storyContext: Maya and Ravi dig into the soil together. 'The soil is hard here,' says Maya. 'We must break it up, mix it, and add compost.' Gopal nods. 'Good soil is the foundation. Without it, even the best seeds will fail.'

points.label: Ploughing
points.text: Turning soil with a plough or tractor breaks up hard ground, mixes nutrients, and removes weeds. Ravi now ploughs 3 times instead of once.

points.label: Levelling
points.text: Smooth, even fields prevent waterlogging and ensure water reaches all plants equally.

points.label: Adding Organic Matter
points.text: Cow manure, compost, and crop residues enrich soil with nitrogen and organic carbon—essential for plant growth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good farming starts with good soil. Break it up, flatten it, and feed it with compost so plants can grow strong.

slides.title: Choosing and Sowing Seeds
slides.storyContext: At the market, Ravi buys high-quality rice seeds certified by the government. Maya asks, 'Why not just any seeds?' Gopal explains the difference between good and bad seeds and the right way to plant them.

points.label: Seed Selection
points.text: Use seeds from healthy, mature plants. High-quality certified seeds germinate faster and give better yields.

points.label: Seed Treatment
points.text: Soak seeds in fungicide (like carbendazim) or use seed balls to protect from soil diseases.

points.label: Sowing Methods
points.text: Broadcasting (scattering): wasteful. Dibbling (placing seeds in holes): uses less seed, gives neat rows, and saves 25% seed.

points.label: Sowing Depth
points.text: Seeds must be buried 2–3 cm deep so roots can push down and shoots can push up.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use good seeds, treat them to stop diseases, and plant them at the right depth and spacing.

slides.title: Nutrients: N, P, K for Growth
slides.storyContext: Three weeks after planting, Ravi notices some rice plants look pale and weak. 'They're hungry,' Gopal says. 'Rice needs nitrogen to grow green leaves, phosphorus to make strong roots, and potassium to make grain. These are called NPK.'

points.label: Nitrogen (N)
points.text: Makes plants green and leafy. Used in urea (46% N). Rice needs 100 kg of N per hectare.

points.label: Phosphorus (P)
points.text: Strengthens roots and helps flowering and grain formation. Found in single superphosphate (16% P).

points.label: Potassium (K)
points.text: Improves grain quality and makes plants resist disease. Found in muriate of potash (60% K).

points.label: Application
points.text: Nitrogen is split: 50% at sowing, 25% at tillering (45 days), 25% at flowering. Phosphorus and potassium are given at sowing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants need three main foods: nitrogen to grow green, phosphorus for roots, and potassium for grain. Give them at the right time.

slides.title: Controlling Weeds, Pests, and Disease
slides.storyContext: By July, the rice field is full of wild grass (weeds) choking the plants. Flies and grasshoppers eat the leaves. Ravi panics, but Gopal shows him chemical and non-chemical methods to save the crop.

points.label: Weed Control
points.text: Manual weeding: pull by hand at 30 and 60 days (best). Chemical: spray 2,4-D herbicide at 30 days to kill broadleaf weeds.

points.label: Pest Management
points.text: Yellow stem borer and armyworm eat rice. Spray monocrotophos or neem oil (1%) to kill them. Use light traps to attract and kill night insects.

points.label: Disease Control
points.text: Bacterial leaf blight and blast are common rice diseases. Spray carbendazim or mancozeb. Remove infected plants to stop spread.

slides.inSimpleWords: Keep the field clean by removing weeds. Kill pests with sprays and traps. Stop diseases before they spread.

slides.title: Water Management
slides.storyContext: In August, the monsoon rains are heavy. The rice field floods. 'Is this good or bad?' asks Maya. Gopal smiles. 'Controlled flooding is good for rice, but too much water causes root rot. Too little causes drought stress. We must manage water carefully.'

points.label: Water Needs
points.text: Rice is a flood-loving crop needing 150 cm of water in 120 days (15 cm every 8 days during growing season).

points.label: Flooding Schedule
points.text: Keep 5 cm water after sowing, increase to 7.5 cm during growing, and drain 2 weeks before harvest.

points.label: Drainage
points.text: Drain excess water to prevent waterlogging, root rot, and fungal disease.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rice loves water but not too much. Keep just the right depth and drain when needed.

image.alt: Water Management — Crop Production and Management

slides.title: Ravi's Harvest Calculation
slides.storyContext: After 120 days of careful management, Ravi's rice is ready. He counts the harvest and talks to Maya about yield.

example.problem: Ravi's plot is 0.5 hectares. Before learning from Gopal, his yield was 3 tonnes per hectare. After good management (soil prep, fertilizer on time, pest control), his yield rose to 5 tonnes per hectare. How much extra rice did he produce? If rice sells for 20 rupees per kg, how much extra money did he earn?
example.solution: Old yield: 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 tonnes = 1500 kg. New yield: 0.5 × 5 = 2.5 tonnes = 2500 kg. Extra rice: 2500 − 1500 = 1000 kg. Extra money: 1000 × 20 = 20,000 rupees. Ravi's income increased by 20,000 rupees!

slides.title: Your Farming Challenge
slides.storyContext: Now it's your turn. A farmer has 1 hectare and wants to grow wheat. Based on what you've learned, list the 5 most important steps to get a good harvest. Then check the answer.

example.problem: You are advising a farmer who has 1 hectare of untouched land. They want to grow wheat with a target yield of 4 tonnes. List 5 management steps in order and explain why each matters.
example.solution: 1. Soil preparation: Plough 2–3 times, level, and mix 5 tonnes compost per hectare to build soil fertility. 2. Seed selection: Buy certified wheat seeds (50 kg per hectare). 3. Fertilizer plan: NPK 100:60:40 per hectare; apply half nitrogen and all phosphorus/potassium at sowing, half nitrogen at flowering. 4. Sowing method: Use a seed drill to sow at 5 cm depth in rows 20 cm apart. 5. Weed and pest control: Manual weed at 30 and 60 days, spray for leaf rust disease. Water 4–5 times in winter wheat season.

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Crop production = soil prep + seed selection + timely nutrients + water + pest control.
Soil must be ploughed, levelled, and enriched with organic matter.
Use certified, treated seeds and sow at the right depth and spacing.
Apply NPK fertilizers on time: N in splits, P and K at sowing.
Manage weeds, pests, and diseases with sprays and farm hygiene.
Give the right water at the right time—not too much, not too little.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good farming is about doing the right thing at the right time: prepare soil, choose good seeds, feed plants on time, control pests, and manage water.

subject: Science
title: Priya's Invisible World
hook: Germs are everywhere—some make us sick, others make our food and medicine. Discover the tiny life that changes the world.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Curious student looking at microbes under a microscope

characters.name: Dr. Sharma
characters.role: Priya's science teacher and local doctor

characters.name: Grandma
characters.role: A traditional food maker who uses fermentation

slides.title: The Invisible Kingdom
slides.storyContext: Priya catches a cold and visits Dr. Sharma. 'You have a viral infection,' he says. At school, she learns that bacteria, viruses, and fungi are everywhere—too small to see but powerful enough to change our lives. Some make us sick, but others help us. Dr. Sharma gives her a microscope slide with bacteria grown on agar. 'Look,' he says. 'These tiny lives are your new world to explore.'

slides.title: What Are Microorganisms?
slides.storyContext: Priya studies her biology textbook and calls Dr. Sharma. 'What exactly am I looking at under the microscope?' He draws a diagram showing the four groups.

points.label: Bacteria
points.text: Single-celled prokaryotes, 1–5 micrometres (μm). Shapes: cocci (round), bacilli (rod), spirilla (spiral). Most do not have a nucleus.

points.label: Viruses
points.text: Not quite alive—they are 20–300 nm, smaller than bacteria, and need a host cell to reproduce. They have DNA or RNA wrapped in protein.

points.label: Fungi
points.text: Eukaryotes (have a nucleus). Include yeasts (1–10 μm, single-celled) and moulds (filaments, multicellular). No chlorophyll; they eat dead matter.

points.label: Algae
points.text: Eukaryotic, have chlorophyll, and make food via photosynthesis. Mostly live in water. Single-celled (like Chlorella) or multicellular (like Spirogyra).

slides.inSimpleWords: Microbes are tiny living things: bacteria and algae are cells, viruses are not quite alive, and fungi eat dead stuff.

slides.title: Helpful Microbes: Making Our Food
slides.storyContext: Priya visits her Grandma, who makes yoghurt every morning. 'How does milk turn into yoghurt?' she asks. Grandma smiles. 'Bacteria! They sour the milk and make it thick. It's been done for thousands of years.'

points.label: Yoghurt & Cheese
points.text: Lactobacillus bacteria ferment lactose (milk sugar) into lactic acid, which curdles the milk. Result: thick yoghurt with tangy taste. Cheese uses Streptococcus and Lactobacillus.

points.label: Bread & Idli
points.text: Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) eats glucose and produces CO₂ gas, making dough rise. Idli uses Lactobacillus and yeast to ferment rice-urad batter.

points.label: Pickling & Fermentation
points.text: Lacto-fermentation uses salt and Lactobacillus to pickle vegetables (achar) and preserve them. It also creates beneficial probiotics.

points.label: Soy Sauce & Sauerkraut
points.text: Aspergillus mould and Bacillus bacteria ferment soy beans into soy sauce; Lactobacillus ferments cabbage into sauerkraut.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria and fungi ferment milk into yoghurt, make bread and idli rise, pickle our vegetables, and make soy sauce—all without cooking.

image.alt: Helpful Microbes: Making Our Food — Microorganisms - Friend and Foe

slides.title: Helpful Microbes: Medicine and Industry
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma shows Priya a bottle of antibiotics. 'This came from a mould called Penicillium,' he says. 'A scientist named Fleming discovered it by accident in 1928. Now we use microbes to make medicines, chemicals, and even biofuel.'

points.label: Antibiotics
points.text: Penicillium notatum produces penicillin, which kills bacteria. Streptomyces produces streptomycin for TB. These microbes produce toxins that hurt bacteria but not us.

points.label: Vaccines
points.text: Bacteria like E. coli are engineered to make human insulin for diabetics. Yeast makes hepatitis B vaccine.

points.label: Biofuel
points.text: Algae and yeast produce bioethanol (fuel) and biogas (methane) from crop waste. Cleaner than fossil fuels.

points.label: Composting
points.text: Bacteria and fungi break down dead plants, leaves, and food waste into compost rich in nitrogen—perfect for gardens.

slides.inSimpleWords: Microbes give us medicines like penicillin, help make insulin for diabetics, produce clean fuel, and turn trash into soil.

image.alt: Helpful Microbes: Medicine and Industry — Microorganisms - Friend and Foe

slides.title: Harmful Microbes: Disease and Spoilage
slides.storyContext: Priya gets food poisoning after eating contaminated food at a street vendor. She's vomiting and has diarrhoea for two days. Dr. Sharma explains: 'Pathogenic bacteria like Salmonella and Vibrio caused this. They produce toxins in your stomach.'

points.label: Bacterial Diseases
points.text: Typhoid (Salmonella typhi), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), TB (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), bacterial pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae).

points.label: Viral Diseases
points.text: COVID-19 (coronavirus), flu (influenza), measles, chickenpox, polio, dengue—viruses enter cells and make copies.

points.label: Fungal Infections
points.text: Ringworm (Tinea), athlete's foot (Candida), thrush. Common in warm, moist skin.

points.label: Food Spoilage
points.text: Bacteria and fungi grow on stale food, meat, and milk, producing bad smell, mold, and toxins (like aflatoxin from Aspergillus).

slides.inSimpleWords: Bad microbes cause typhoid, cholera, flu, and infections. They also make food smell and taste rotten.

image.alt: Harmful Microbes: Disease and Spoilage — Microorganisms - Friend and Foe

slides.title: How Diseases Spread
slides.storyContext: During the COVID-19 lockdown, Priya learns why spreading germs matters. Dr. Sharma explains the different routes.

points.label: Airborne
points.text: Flu, COVID-19, TB. Spread via droplets when coughing or sneezing.

points.label: Waterborne
points.text: Cholera, typhoid. Spread via contaminated drinking water.

points.label: Foodborne
points.text: Salmonella (undercooked eggs, meat), Listeria (unpasteurised cheese). Grow when food is not stored cold.

points.label: Contact
points.text: Ringworm, chickenpox, COVID-19 (touching infected skin or surfaces). Wash hands to break the chain.

slides.inSimpleWords: Germs spread through air, water, food, and touch. Keep clean, cook food, and store it cold to stop them.

slides.title: Keeping Microbes Safe and Away
slides.storyContext: Priya's school conducts a hygiene day. She learns how to stop bad microbes while protecting good ones.

points.label: Disinfection
points.text: Heat (boiling kills bacteria), UV light, and antiseptics (like alcohol, bleach) kill microbes on surfaces.

points.label: Sanitation
points.text: Proper sewage treatment, clean drinking water, and waste disposal prevent waterborne disease.

points.label: Vaccination
points.text: Vaccines train the immune system to recognise viruses (like measles, polio) and fight them before they spread.

points.label: Preservation
points.text: Refrigeration slows microbial growth. Salt, sugar, and acid (pickling) preserve food. Pasteurisation (65°C for 30 min) kills pathogens in milk.

slides.inSimpleWords: Boil water, keep things clean, wash your hands, get vaccinated, and store food cold to stay healthy.

image.alt: Keeping Microbes Safe and Away — Microorganisms - Friend and Foe

slides.title: A Yoghurt Experiment
slides.storyContext: Priya makes yoghurt at home with her Grandma. They measure temperature and time to understand fermentation.

example.problem: Grandma heats 1 litre of milk to 80°C for 15 minutes to kill bad bacteria, then cools it to 45°C. She adds a spoonful of starter yoghurt containing Lactobacillus (about 10^8 bacteria per mL). If the bacteria double every 30 minutes, how many bacteria will be in the yoghurt after 6 hours? Express as a power of 2.
example.solution: Initial bacteria: 10^8. Doubling time: 30 minutes. In 6 hours = 360 minutes, the bacteria double 360 ÷ 30 = 12 times. Final count: 10^8 × 2^12 = 10^8 × 4096 = 4.096 × 10^11 bacteria. After 6 hours at 45°C, the yoghurt thickens and sours as lactic acid builds up. Temperature is key: too hot (>50°C) kills the bacteria; too cold (<40°C) slows growth.

slides.title: Design a Food Safety Plan
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother is catering a wedding with 500 people. She asks Priya to plan how to keep the food safe from harmful bacteria from morning prep to evening serving.

example.problem: A caterer is preparing rice, curries, and paneer dishes for 500 people. Serving will start at 6 PM. Design a food safety plan that includes prep time, storage, and serving. Consider risks: Clostridium, Salmonella, Staphylococcus.
example.solution: 1. Prep (3 AM): Cook rice and curries to 75°C to kill all pathogens. Let paneer cook to 65°C. 2. Hot hold (3–5 AM): Keep cooked food above 65°C in insulated boxes or hot-water bath to prevent recontamination and new growth. 3. Transport (5–5:45 PM): Keep hot food in thermal containers; do not let it sit at room temperature (bacterial danger zone 4–60°C). 4. Serve (6 PM): Ladle hot food onto clean plates. Do not re-use serving utensils; use fresh ones. Keep raw onions and salads separate from cooked food. 5. Result: Food stays hot, bacteria cannot grow above 65°C, and cross-contamination is prevented.

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Microbes include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and algae—most too small to see without a microscope.
Good microbes make yoghurt, bread, beer, medicines, and biofuel. They also decompose dead matter.
Bad microbes cause typhoid, cholera, TB, flu, and food poisoning.
Diseases spread through air, water, food, and contact. Wash hands, cook food, and store it cold.
Vaccines, sanitation, heat, and antiseptics kill harmful microbes and keep us safe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Microbes are everywhere: some make food and medicine, others cause disease. Keep clean, cook well, and vaccinate to stay healthy.

subject: Science
title: Arjun's Fossil Fuel Journey
hook: Coal and oil are ancient energy—formed from dinosaurs and plants millions of years ago. See where your electricity and petrol come from.

characters.name: Engineer Verma
characters.role: Works at a thermal power plant

slides.title: The Power Plant Visit
slides.storyContext: Arjun's school organises a trip to a thermal power plant near his city. Engineer Verma, who works there, shows him towering cooling towers and long conveyor belts bringing black coal. 'This coal,' says Verma, 'is 300 million years old. It came from forests that sank beneath the earth and turned to stone.' Arjun's eyes widen. 'So our electricity comes from dinosaur-age plants?' Verma nods. 'Exactly. And petrol comes from even older sea creatures.'

slides.title: What Are Fossil Fuels? Formation of Coal
slides.storyContext: Engineer Verma takes Arjun to the geology museum and shows him rock layers. 'Look,' he points. 'The bottom layers are the oldest. This coal formed in the Carboniferous period, 300 million years ago, when swamps covered the earth.'

points.label: Formation Process
points.text: Ancient forests died and sank into swamps → buried under mud and sand → heat and pressure for millions of years → carbon-rich remains turned to coal.

points.label: Coal Ranks (by carbon %)
points.text: Peat (50% C, young), Lignite (65% C, soft), Bituminous (85% C, hard, used in power plants), Anthracite (95% C, hardest, best quality).

points.label: Why India?
points.text: India has vast coal reserves in Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Jharkhand. Coal powers 50% of India's electricity.

points.label: Energy Content
points.text: Bituminous coal: 25–30 MJ/kg. This is why burning 1 kg coal heats your home for hours.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coal is fossilised plant matter, buried and squeezed for 300 million years. More buried time → harder coal → more energy.

slides.title: Extracting Coal: Mining Methods
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks Verma, 'How do they get coal out of the ground?' Verma drives him to a coal mine and shows him two methods.

points.label: Underground Mining
points.text: Used when coal is deep (>100 m). Miners dig shafts and tunnels. Dangerous: risk of collapse, gas explosions, and flooding. Deep mines in Odisha.

points.label: Open-Pit (Surface) Mining
points.text: Used when coal is shallow (<100 m). Remove topsoil and rock (overburden), dig out coal. Faster and safer but destroys the landscape. Most common in India.

points.label: Environmental Cost
points.text: Mining leaves large pits, pollutes groundwater, and removes forests. Rehabilitation of mined land is expensive and slow.

points.label: Worker Hazards
points.text: Silicosis (lung disease from coal dust), accidents, exposure to methane gas.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coal is dug from deep mines or open pits. Digging is dangerous and harms the land, but coal is vital for power.

image.alt: Extracting Coal: Mining Methods — Coal and Petroleum

slides.title: From Coal to Electricity
slides.storyContext: Verma takes Arjun to the power plant's control room. 'Watch,' he says, pointing at screens. 'Coal is crushed into powder, burnt in a furnace, and the heat boils water to make steam. Steam spins turbines, which turn generators. That makes electricity for your home.'

points.label: Combustion
points.text: Coal (C, S, H) burns in furnace: C + O₂ → CO₂ + heat (393 kJ/mol). Heats water from 25°C to 100°C and creates steam at high pressure.

points.label: Steam Turbine
points.text: Pressurised steam (200–300 atm, 400–600°C) drives turbine blades, spinning at 3000 rpm.

points.label: Generator
points.text: Turbine rotates coils in a magnetic field, inducing alternating current (AC). Step-up transformer raises voltage (11 kV → 220 kV) for transmission.

points.label: Efficiency
points.text: Only 35–40% of coal's energy becomes electricity; the rest is lost as heat in cooling towers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coal burns to heat water into steam. Steam spins turbines. Turbines turn generators that make electricity.

slides.title: Petroleum: Formation and Extraction
slides.storyContext: Arjun's father is a geologist. He shows Arjun maps of oil fields in the Arabian Sea. 'Oil formed from tiny sea creatures and algae that died 200–300 million years ago,' he explains. 'Heat and pressure turned them into liquid hydrocarbons.'

points.label: Formation
points.text: Marine organisms (plankton, algae) → buried in sediment → heat (50–90°C) and pressure → oil and natural gas (kerogen cracking).

points.label: Conditions Required
points.text: Must have: source rock (organic-rich sediment), permeable rock (sand/limestone) to hold oil, impermeable cap rock to trap it.

points.label: Major Oil Fields
points.text: India: Bombay High, Western Geophysical, Rajasthan. Global: Saudi Arabia, Russia, USA, Iraq.

points.label: Extraction
points.text: Drilling: bore a well to the oil reservoir. Pumping: oil rises due to pressure or is pumped up. Typical well: 500 m–2 km deep.

slides.inSimpleWords: Oil is fossilised sea creatures. It's trapped under rock layers and pumped up through wells.

slides.title: Refining Crude Oil into Fuels
slides.storyContext: Arjun visits an oil refinery. Black crude oil arrives by tanker. 'This is useless as-is,' says the refinery manager. 'We separate it into petrol, diesel, kerosene, and fuel oil. It's called fractional distillation.'

points.label: Crude Oil Composition
points.text: Mix of hydrocarbons: C₅–C₄₀ (alkanes, cycloalkanes, aromatics) + impurities (sulfur, nitrogen, metals). Density: 0.8–0.9 g/cm³.

points.label: Fractional Distillation
points.text: Heat crude to 350°C, send vapours into a fractionating column (hot at bottom, cold at top). Different molecules condense at different heights based on boiling point.

points.label: Fractions (Top to Bottom)
points.text: Petroleum gas (C₁–C₄, 40°C), petrol/gasoline (C₅–C₁₀, 60–180°C), kerosene (C₁₀–C₁₆, 180–300°C), diesel (C₁₆–C₂₀, >300°C), fuel oil, bitumen (residue).

points.label: Uses
points.text: Petrol: cars, scooters. Diesel: trucks, buses, pumps. Kerosene: stoves, lamps, aviation fuel. Fuel oil: power plants, ships.

slides.inSimpleWords: Crude oil is heated and separated into fuels: petrol for cars, diesel for trucks, kerosene for lamps, based on boiling points.

image.alt: Refining Crude Oil into Fuels — Coal and Petroleum

slides.title: Environmental Impact: Pollution and Climate Change
slides.storyContext: Sameer, an environmental scientist, meets Arjun at the power plant. 'Coal and oil are cheap energy,' he says, 'but they cost us the climate. Burning them releases CO₂ and pollutes the air we breathe.'

points.label: Air Pollution
points.text: Burning coal releases SO₂ (sulfur dioxide) and NO₂ (nitrogen dioxide), causing acid rain. Soot (particulates <10 μm) enters lungs and causes asthma, bronchitis.

points.label: Climate Change
points.text: C + O₂ → CO₂ (45% of global emissions). CO₂ is a greenhouse gas: it traps heat, raising Earth's temperature. 1990: 350 ppm; 2024: 420 ppm.

points.label: Oil Spills
points.text: Tanker accidents (Exxon Valdez: 11 million gallons) kill marine life and poison water for decades.

points.label: Non-Renewable
points.text: Oil reserves: ~50 years at current use. Coal: ~100 years. Once burned, they're gone forever.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coal and oil pollute the air, cause climate change by releasing CO₂, and damage oceans if they spill. They're also running out.

slides.title: Alternatives: Renewable Energy
slides.storyContext: Sameer is optimistic. 'We don't have to rely on coal and oil forever,' he tells Arjun. 'The sun, wind, and water can power our future without pollution.'

points.label: Solar Power
points.text: Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight (1000 W/m²) directly to electricity. India: 60 GW solar capacity (2024), target 500 GW by 2030.

points.label: Wind Power
points.text: Wind turbines turn kinetic energy into electricity. India: 40 GW wind capacity, mostly in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.

points.label: Hydropower
points.text: Water behind dams drives turbines. India: 50 GW hydro, 12% of total electricity.

points.label: Biomass & Biogas
points.text: Burn agricultural waste (crop residue, cow dung) for heat/power. Clean and renewable if managed sustainably.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solar, wind, water, and biomass are clean energies that won't run out and don't pollute.

slides.title: Coal vs. Solar: A Cost Calculation
slides.storyContext: Arjun's school is considering switching to solar power. He calculates the savings.

example.problem: The school's diesel generator uses 50 litres per month at Rs. 100 per litre, costing Rs. 5,000/month (Rs. 60,000/year). A solar setup costs Rs. 5,00,000 upfront and requires Rs. 2,000/year maintenance. How many years until solar pays for itself? Assume no increase in diesel price.
example.solution: Annual diesel cost: 60,000. Annual solar cost (after upfront): 2,000. Savings per year: 60,000 − 2,000 = 58,000. Payback time: 500,000 ÷ 58,000 = 8.6 years. So in about 8-9 years, the solar setup has saved more than it cost. After that, the school pays only 2,000/year. Over a 20-year solar panel lifespan, total savings: (60,000 × 20) − 500,000 − (2,000 × 20) = 1,200,000 − 500,000 − 40,000 = 660,000 rupees!

slides.title: Design an Energy Mix for India
slides.storyContext: The government asks your class to design India's energy mix for 2050. You must balance power needs (target: 1,200 GW), cost, and climate.

example.problem: India's current energy capacity: 400 GW (coal 54%, hydro 12%, wind 10%, solar 15%, gas 7%, nuclear 2%). By 2050, India needs 1,200 GW. Coal reserves will last ~80 years (to 2100). Design a mix that: (a) meets 1,200 GW, (b) keeps coal <30%, (c) uses renewables >60%, (d) adds 100 GW nuclear. Justify your choices.
example.solution: Target 1,200 GW capacity by 2050: Coal 300 GW (25%, decline from 216 GW), Solar 400 GW (33%, massive growth), Wind 250 GW (21%, exploit coastal and highland zones), Hydro 80 GW (7%, max potential), Nuclear 100 GW (8%, new reactors), Gas/Biomass 70 GW (6%, flexible backup). Why: (1) Coal declines steadily, extending reserves. (2) Solar and wind grow 5-fold, harnessing free renewable resources and reducing cost via scale. (3) Nuclear provides baseload (24/7) power without CO₂. (4) Hydro and gas are dispatchable backup for when sun and wind fail. Result: India eliminates coal by 2100, avoids climate targets, and creates millions of green jobs. Cost: high upfront (Rs. 10 lakh crore), but lower fuel costs long-term.

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Coal and petroleum are fossil fuels formed from ancient organisms over 200–300 million years.
Coal is mined (underground or open-pit) and burnt to heat water, driving steam turbines to generate electricity.
Crude oil is extracted by drilling, then refined (fractional distillation) into petrol, diesel, kerosene, and fuel oil.
Burning coal and oil releases CO₂, pollutes air with SO₂ and NO₂, and causes climate change.
Fossil fuels are non-renewable and will run out. Solar, wind, hydro, and biomass are clean alternatives.
Energy efficiency and renewable energy are the keys to a sustainable future.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coal and oil come from fossils buried for millions of years. We burn them for energy, but they pollute and will run out. Solar and wind are the clean future.
